pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–10 years

- **Topic:** Ecology Vocabulary (producer, consumer, predator, prey, decomposer)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'Animals, including humans'):** pupils identify producers, predators and prey when constructing and interpreting food chains — the vocabulary is the named backbone of that objective.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-LS2-1):** the model of matter movement among plants, animals, DECOMPOSERS and the environment names the decomposer role explicitly; producer/consumer roles underpin the whole PE.

- **Operational details:** This is a LANGUAGE topic — the goal is precise, durable command of the role words, each tied to its function in the flow of energy/matter. The five core roles: PRODUCER (makes its own food from sunlight — green plants/algae), CONSUMER (eats other organisms; sub-roles herbivore/carnivore/omnivore), PREDATOR (a consumer that hunts), PREY (what is hunted), DECOMPOSER (breaks down dead matter, returning nutrients — fungi, bacteria, some minibeasts). The key discriminations: producer vs consumer (self-feeding vs eating others), predator vs prey (a ROLE in a relationship, not a fixed identity — a mouse is prey to an owl but predator to a beetle), and decomposer as a distinct role often forgotten.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). Success = correctly labels each organism in a familiar scene with its role(s), and understands predator/prey as relational — the same animal can be both depending on the pairing.
bestPractices: Bind each word to its FUNCTION in the flow of food, not to a list of example animals — 'producer = makes its own food from sunlight' travels; 'producer = plants' breaks the moment algae or a decomposer appears.
Teach predator/prey explicitly as relational roles using a chain of three (beetle–mouse–owl) so the middle organism is visibly both at once.
Give decomposers equal billing — they are the most-forgotten role; show them returning nutrients to the soil so the child sees why the role matters, not just names it.
Use retrieval sorting (drag organisms into role bins) soon after introduction to move the words from recognition to recall.
Contrast near-synonyms deliberately: consumer vs predator (all predators are consumers, not all consumers are predators) and herbivore/carnivore/omnivore as sub-kinds of consumer.
keyRepresentations: Annotated habitat scene with each organism tagged by role — the canonical vocabulary anchor
Three-organism chain (beetle → mouse → owl) showing the middle organism as both predator and prey
Role bins / sorting mat: producer | consumer | decomposer
Decomposer close-up: fungi on a log with nutrient arrows returning to soil
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 'producer' means a factory/maker in the human sense, or that producers are 'the strong ones', rather than organisms that make their own food from sunlight.
Treating predator and prey as fixed identities — not realising the same animal is prey to one organism and predator to another.
Forgetting decomposers entirely, or thinking dead things just disappear rather than being broken down and recycled.
Confusing consumer and predator — assuming any animal that eats is a 'predator', missing that herbivores are consumers but not predators.

learn.summary: Build durable, precise command of ecology role vocabulary (producer, consumer, predator, prey, herbivore, carnivore, omnivore, decomposer) for 8–10s by binding each word to its FUNCTION in the flow of food rather than to a fixed list of example animals. The central discriminations are producer vs consumer (makes its own food vs eats others), predator vs prey as RELATIONAL roles (the same animal can be both depending on the pairing), and decomposer as a distinct, frequently-forgotten role that returns nutrients to the soil. Work across a labelled habitat scene (anchoring words to visible organisms), active sorting for retrieval, and spoken use-in-context to reveal whether the learner truly owns the relational and recycling meanings.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal role glossary over one habitat scene
feedback: If a learner refuses to call the mouse prey because 'it's a predator', show it eating the beetle (predator) AND being eaten by the owl (prey): predator/prey name a relationship, not a fixed type.

If a learner calls the fungi a consumer, contrast it with an ordinary consumer — the decomposer breaks dead matter down and returns nutrients to the soil for producers; that recycling is what 'decomposer' names.

If a learner names the biggest or first animal the 'producer', anchor 'producer' to making its own food from sunlight — the green plants in this scene, the oak AND the grass (and algae in general), qualify; the animals do not.
activities.rationale: Vocabulary anchored to visible, labelled organisms lets each role word be met against its function; colour-coding producers/consumers/decomposers and a three-link chain (beetle→mouse→owl) make the relational middle organism visible at once. Standards name these roles as the backbone of food-chain work.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'Animals, including humans' requires pupils to identify producers, predators and prey when constructing and interpreting food chains.
NGSS 5-LS2-1 names decomposers explicitly as part of the model of matter movement among plants, animals, decomposers and the environment.
learnerActions: Study a single rich woodland scene with named organisms (oak and grass, rabbit, mouse, fox, owl, beetle, fungi on a dead log).

Tap/point to each organism and reveal its role bound to its function: oak and grass = 'PRODUCER — makes its own food from sunlight'; rabbit = 'CONSUMER — eats plants; here it is PREY to the fox'; fox = 'PREDATOR — hunts the rabbit'; fungi = 'DECOMPOSER — breaks down the dead and returns nutrients to the soil'.

Tap the mouse and see it flagged BOTH as PREY (to the owl above) AND PREDATOR (to the beetle below); note it is also shown feeding on grass seeds, so it eats both plants and animals. Answer a lift-the-flap question 'so is the mouse a predator or prey?' and then check it against 'both — it depends who you compare it to'.
Drill into the fungi close-up to see nutrients returning to the soil, so the decomposer role is understood as recycling, not just 'eating dead things'.
activities.intendedInsight: The five core role words name precise functions in the flow of food, and predator/prey name a relationship rather than a fixed identity — the same organism can be predator in one pairing and prey in another.

activities.title: Sort organisms into roles, then flip the pairing
feedback: Give immediate feedback on each placement; when a learner keeps an organism in a fixed predator/prey bin after the partner changes, re-show both pairings so the relationship — not the animal — drives the label.
If all predators are placed but a herbivore is also called a 'predator', point out all predators are consumers but not all consumers are predators.
If a learner labels the mouse a carnivore because it hunts the beetle, point to it also feeding on grass seeds in the scene — eating both plants and animals is what 'omnivore' names.
activities.rationale: Active retrieval soon after introduction is intended to consolidate the words and self-test them; the deliberate contrast of near-synonyms (consumer vs predator) and the flip-the-pairing move target the specific discriminations learners confuse.
learnerActions: Drag or place each organism into role bins: producer | consumer | decomposer.
Within a shown pairing, assign predator and prey (e.g. fox–rabbit, owl–mouse).
Take a 'flip the pairing' twist: when the mouse's partner changes from the owl to the beetle, reclassify it from prey to predator, and explain why.

Sort consumers into sub-kinds — herbivore, carnivore, omnivore — using a correct example for each where the scene supports it (rabbit = herbivore; owl = carnivore; the mouse, which the scene shows eating both the beetle and grass seeds, = omnivore). The fox is shown only eating meat here, but real foxes also eat fruit and berries, so they are usually called omnivores. Do not mark 'carnivore' as the only right answer for the fox.
activities.intendedInsight: Retrieval sorting is intended to move the words from recognition to recall, and reclassifying the same animal when its partner changes makes the relational nature of predator/prey concrete; herbivore/carnivore/omnivore are sub-kinds of consumer.

activities.title: Talk me through who's who — spoken use in context
feedback: Expected full use: oak = producer; caterpillar = primary consumer/herbivore and prey; blue tit = consumer/predator of caterpillars, prey to the sparrowhawk, and the likely omnivore here (in real life blue tits also eat seeds, especially in winter; call it an omnivore only if the learner gives that reason or the scene shows it); sparrowhawk = predator/carnivore; fungi = decomposer breaking down the dead log and recycling nutrients to the soil.
If the learner uses terms as loose labels, confuses producer with an animal, or treats predator/prey as fixed types, re-anchor each word to its function and re-run a changed pairing.

A field-ecologist persona can probe Socratically ('you called the blue tit a predator — is it also prey to anything here?') to elicit the relational insight through dialogue, as a deepening step after the words are met against the scene.
activities.rationale: Dialogue and spoken use in context surface the misconceptions that recognition tasks hide — particularly the relational nature of predator/prey and the decomposer's recycling role — and check transfer to a new organism.
learnerActions: Face a woodland scene: oak trees, caterpillars, blue tits, a sparrowhawk, fungi on a dead log.
Talk through who's who and what happens to energy and to the dead wood, using whichever words fit: producer, consumer, predator, prey, herbivore, carnivore, omnivore, decomposer.

Answer probing questions: 'You called the blue tit a predator — is it also prey to anything in this wood?'; 'What does the fungus do that an ordinary consumer does not?'; 'Which animal here could be an omnivore, and why?'; 'Which organism is the producer, and what earns it that name?'
Transfer the vocabulary to a fresh organism not yet discussed.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct USE in context (not recited definitions) reveals whether the learner holds predator/prey as relational, keeps decomposer distinct from consumer, and distinguishes herbivore/carnivore/omnivore.

constraints: Bind each word to its function in the flow of food ('producer = makes its own food from sunlight'), not to example animals ('producer = plants'), which breaks the moment algae or a decomposer appears.
Give decomposers equal billing — they are the most-forgotten role; show them returning nutrients to the soil so the learner sees why the role matters, not just names it.

Recognition/sorting and multiple-choice tasks check and consolidate the words but do not by themselves elicit independent, spoken use in context; include a use-in-context or dialogue task to confirm the relational and recycling meanings are owned.

A tap-to-reveal picture glossary is a strong anchor for first meeting the words, but a fixed labelled scene only shows pre-set pairings; use the flip-the-pairing sort and spoken transfer to a fresh organism so predator/prey is understood as relational beyond the one scene.

Treat herbivore/carnivore/omnivore as sub-kinds of consumer and contrast consumer vs predator deliberately (all predators are consumers; not all consumers are predators). Only assign a sub-kind label when the scene actually shows the relevant feeding (e.g. omnivore requires the scene to depict eating both plants and animals, as with the mouse eating the beetle and grass seeds).
Treat every green plant in a scene as a producer, not just one named plant (the oak and the grass both qualify); anchor the label to making food from sunlight, not to size or prominence.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a 3D interactive 'poor' claiming '3D adds nothing' and that vocabulary 'needs clear labelled organisms, not spatial manipulation'. This comparative-necessity claim is not established by the sources; it is softened to an affordance note (a labelled scene suffices for anchoring role words; navigation cost is a design trade-off, not a proven universal).

One source claim ('Predator and prey are relational roles... decomposers are a distinct, frequently-omitted role') is marked verified:false in the row; the relational and recycling teaching points rest partly on it, so they are presented as pedagogical guidance rather than cited fact and are not attached as sourceClaims.

The original row's diagnostic correctAnswer did not resolve its own 'which animal could be an omnivore' probe; corrected activity 3 names the blue tit (eats insects and seeds/berries) as the omnivore candidate so the probe has a modelled answer.

The glossary scene (activity 1) originally depicted the mouse only as predator of the beetle; to make its omnivore classification in activity 2 coherent, the scene is now stated to also show it feeding on grass seeds. This is a design addition for internal consistency, not a sourced fact.
The scene lists grass as well as the oak; both are producers, so producer feedback was corrected to name both rather than 'only the oak'.

probeDeeper: You called the blue tit a predator — is it also prey to anything in this wood?
What does the fungus do that an ordinary consumer does not?
Use 'omnivore' correctly — which animal here could be one, and why?
Which organism is the producer, and what earns it that name?
assess.correctAnswer: Uses the terms accurately in context: oak = producer; caterpillar = primary consumer / herbivore and prey; blue tit = consumer / predator of caterpillars and prey to the sparrowhawk; sparrowhawk = predator / carnivore; fungi = decomposer breaking down the dead log and recycling nutrients back to the soil. Relational terms (predator/prey) are attached to the right pairs, and the decomposer's recycling role is stated.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 'predator' and 'prey' as permanent identities rather than roles — the blue tit 'is a predator, so it can't be prey'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the blue tit eats caterpillars (predator) AND is eaten by the sparrowhawk (prey); predator/prey name a relationship, not a fixed type.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to call the blue tit prey even though the sparrowhawk eats it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Collapses 'decomposer' into 'consumer' — 'it just eats the dead wood' — missing the recycling-nutrients meaning.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the fungus with an ordinary consumer: it breaks dead matter down and returns nutrients to the soil for producers — that recycling role is what 'decomposer' names.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the fungus a consumer, with no mention of breaking material down or returning nutrients to the soil.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misapplies 'producer' — uses it for the first/biggest animal rather than the plant that makes its own food.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor 'producer' to making one's own food by photosynthesis — only the oak qualifies here.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the caterpillar or the sparrowhawk the producer.

responseLevels.gap: Uses the terms as loose labels; confuses producer with an animal, or predator/prey as fixed types.
responseLevels.full: Uses all the terms accurately in the scene, applies predator/prey relationally (one animal both), distinguishes the decomposer's recycling role, and transfers the vocabulary to a fresh organism.
responseLevels.partial: Places most terms correctly but treats predator/prey as fixed identities, or blurs decomposer with consumer.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Present a woodland scene: oak trees, caterpillars, blue tits, a sparrowhawk, and fungi growing on a dead log. Say: 'Talk me through who's who here, and what happens to energy and to the dead wood — use whichever of these words fit: producer, consumer, predator, prey, herbivore, carnivore, omnivore, decomposer.' Listen for correct use, not recited definitions.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who half-owns the words treats 'predator' and 'prey' as fixed identities (so the blue tit can't be both), collapses 'decomposer' into 'just eats dead things', or muddles herbivore/carnivore. Correct USE reveals the relational nature (one animal is predator to one thing, prey to another) and the decomposer's distinct recycling role.
